episode.broadcastScript:
This is The Innovation Pulse for Tuesday, March 17, 2026. Here's what's happening in A.I. and higher education.
-
Today, a UK company offers free A.I. access to university students when institutions purchase staff licenses, addressing a growing digital divide.
-
In Insights and Trends today, ICS.AI has launched a model that gives UK university students free access to institutional A.I. tools when universities purchase staff licenses.

According to IT Brief UK, fewer than five percent of the UK's 2.9 million higher education students currently have access to structured institutional A.I. tools. Meanwhile, 57 percent of employers report significant A.I. skills gaps in their workforce.

ICS.AI's CEO Martin Neale describes this access gap as a potential defining driver of graduate employability. For an institution with 20,000 students, annual spending on commercial A.I. services can reach millions, making universal access financially prohibitive for many institutions.

The company emphasizes governance, audit trails, and compliance controls in its platform. The bundled approach positions A.I. literacy as basic educational infrastructure, similar to internet access or library resources. The model addresses the cost barrier that has created a divide between students who can afford individual A.I. subscriptions and those who cannot.
-
In Case Studies, Wychwood School in Oxford has launched A.I. Futures Oxford, offering an A-level in Artificial Intelligence for students aged 16 and over.

According to IT Brief UK, the program operates outside normal school hours, allowing students to stay at their current schools while adding A.I. education. The micro-school model provides specialized A.I. instruction without requiring students to transfer institutions.
-
Turning to Ethical A.I., University of Amsterdam lecturer Nicos Starreveld argues that excessive focus on A.I.-secure testing undermines trust between faculty and students.

According to Folia.nl, Starreveld advocates for emphasizing student learning and well-being over assessment security. He suggests A.I.-secure assignments should focus on affective learning domains rather than attempting to detect or prevent all A.I. use.
-
In Insights and Trends, a Jobs for the Future survey found 70 percent of students use A.I. weekly for education, up from 59 percent in 2024.

According to Inside Higher Ed, 48 percent of students seek A.I. guidance from social media versus only 23 percent from educational institutions. This indicates students prefer informal learning channels despite increased institutional training offerings.
-
In Beyond Ed, the White House released a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence with legislative recommendations for Congress.

According to the Center for Data Innovation, the framework emphasizes innovation over restrictive regulation. The Center praised the framework for addressing legitimate concerns while avoiding barriers to A.I. deployment and calling for federal preemption of conflicting state laws.
-
That's today's Innovation Pulse. Full coverage and source links at innovating higher ed dot com.

stories.headline: NSF Awards $11M for K-12 A.I. Teacher Training
stories.summary: The National Science Foundation awarded $11 million to the Computer Science Teachers Association to train 2,500-3,000 K-12 educators in A.I. and computer science foundations, according to Mirage News. The program will operate across seven states and aims to reach 500,000-600,000 students over two years.
